{{Short description|Topological structure of Euclidean space}}{{Duplication|date=June 2025|dupe=Real_coordinate_space#Topological_properties}}

In mathematics, and especially [[general topology]], the '''Euclidean topology''' is the [[natural topology]] induced on <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^n</math> by the [[Euclidean distance|Euclidean metric]].

==Definition==

The [[Euclidean norm]] on <math>\R^n</math> is the non-negative function <math>\|\cdot\| : \R^n \to \R</math> defined by
<math display=block>\left\|\left(p_1, \ldots, p_n\right)\right\| ~:=~ \sqrt{p_1^2 + \cdots + p_n^2}.</math>

Like all [[Norm (mathematics)|norms]], it induces a canonical [[Metric (mathematics)|metric]] defined by <math>d(p, q) = \|p - q\|.</math> The metric <math>d : \R^n \times \R^n \to \R</math> induced by the [[Euclidean norm]] is called the [[Euclidean metric]] or the [[Euclidean distance]] and the distance between points <math>p = \left(p_1, \ldots, p_n\right)</math> and <math>q = \left(q_1, \ldots, q_n\right)</math> is 
<math display=block>d(p, q) ~=~ \|p - q\| ~=~ \sqrt{\left(p_1 - q_1\right)^2 + \left(p_2 - q_2\right)^2 + \cdots + \left(p_i - q_i\right)^2 + \cdots + \left(p_n - q_n\right)^2}.</math>

In any [[metric space]], the [[Ball (mathematics)|open balls]] form a [[Base (topology)|base]] for a topology on that space.<ref>[[Metric space|Metric space#Open and closed sets.2C topology and convergence]]</ref> 
The Euclidean topology on <math>\R^n</math> is the topology {{em|generated}} by these balls. 
In other words, the open sets of the Euclidean topology on <math>\R^n</math> are given by (arbitrary) unions of the open balls <math>B_r(p)</math> defined as <math>B_r(p) := \left\{x \in \R^n : d(p,x) < r\right\},</math> for all real <math>r > 0</math> and all <math>p \in \R^n,</math> where <math>d</math> is the Euclidean metric.

==Properties==

When endowed with this topology, the real line <math>\R</math> is a [[T5 space|T<sub>5</sub> space]]. 
Given two subsets say <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> of <math>\R</math> with <math>\overline{A} \cap B = A \cap \overline{B} = \varnothing,</math> where <math>\overline{A}</math> denotes the [[Closure (topology)|closure]] of <math>A,</math> there exist open sets <math>S_A</math> and <math>S_B</math> with <math>A \subseteq S_A</math> and <math>B \subseteq S_B</math> such that <math>S_A \cap S_B = \varnothing.</math><ref name="CEIT">{{Citation|last=Steen|first=L. A.|title=[[Counterexamples in Topology]]|year=1995|last2=Seebach|first2=J. A.|publisher=Dover|ISBN=0-486-68735-X}}</ref>
